title: Orsen and the Glasshouse
premise: Sebastian Nakamura, a translator who has spent her life rendering other people's words while losing her mother's Japanese one borrowed word at a time, returns to her estranged family's glasshouse nursery for a funeral she almost skipped. A stranger named Orsen greets mourners with a family name nobody uses anymore and seems to know the house's secrets better than any of them. As Sebastian translates the dead woman's letters, she uncovers that Orsen is the unacknowledged daughter of the grandfather whose inheritance quietly shaped every sibling's life. Confronting the family's arranged silence, Sebastian must choose whether to claim her own fractured identity or keep living as a tenant in it; in the end, she gives Orsen the glasshouse and, for the first time, speaks a full sentence in her mother's tongue.
about_author: Hazel Okonkwo is a former botanical illustrator who grew up above her family's plant shop in Lagos before moving to England to study comparative literature. Her fiction explores how families inherit silence as readily as land.

chapters.title: The Tenant
chapters.summary: Sebastian's POV. At her mother's funeral, Sebastian drifts through rituals in two half-languages, translating condolences she cannot feel. A stranger named Orsen arrives uninvited, greeting relatives by an old family name no one uses. When Sebastian asks who invited her, Orsen says only that she was expected. Emotional beat: dislocation sharpening into unease.

chapters.title: What the Glass Remembers
chapters.summary: Alternating POV between Sebastian and Orsen. Sorting her mother's effects in the glasshouse nursery, Sebastian finds letters addressed to a name she doesn't recognize—her grandfather's first family. Orsen, meanwhile, watches the house from a rented room, rehearsing what she came to say. Emotional beat: curiosity curdling into dread as the two women orbit the same secret.

chapters.title: A Name Nobody Uses
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV, closing on Sebastian's. At a tense family dinner, Orsen reveals herself: the grandfather's unacknowledged daughter, conceived in the glasshouse he built. The siblings' carefully arranged inheritances begin to crack; Sebastian's brother demands she leave, but Sebastian defends her, realizing the family's silence cost her own language and selfhood. Emotional beat: confrontation—the arc's climax.

chapters.title: Rootstock
chapters.summary: Sebastian's POV. Weeks later, Sebastian finishes translating her mother's letters and reads them aloud to Orsen among the plants. She signs over the glasshouse, refusing the inheritance-as-ownership her family worshipped, and chooses found kinship instead. In the final scene she speaks a complete sentence in Japanese to Orsen across the glass. Emotional beat: release, belonging, quiet resolution.
